content:
President Trump traveled to San Antonio, Texas on Wednesday to campaign for Republican Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton, amid a growing controversy over his repeated comments about Paxton's appearance.

The controversy was thrown back into the spotlight on September 30 when The New York Times published a leaked recording in which Paxton privately complained that Trump's speech at a Dallas Republican midterm event could hurt his campaign.

The president himself has yet to respond to the recording.

While stumping for Paxton in Denton, Texas last week, Trump described Paxton as "a real pain in the ass sometimes" and questioned whether he was in attendance — even though he was — before walking it back and calling him "the best attorney general in the country."

On the final night of a Republican midterm event on September 10, Trump said: "I said to him, 'Ken, I don't want to embarrass you, but we have too many differences... I'm not sure I like your look, I don't know if I like your clothing, I don't like your speaking.'"

The night before, Trump had already said that Paxton "maybe doesn't dress as well, maybe doesn't speak as well, and maybe is not the best-looking guy I've ever seen."

Speaking from the Oval Office in early September about Paxton's Democratic opponent James Talarico, Trump said: "We have a guy named Ken Paxton. Some people don't like the way he dresses, some people don't like the way he gives interviews, some people don't like the way he talks."

With less than five weeks to go until the November midterms, the Texas Senate race remains tight. According to the latest polls from The New York Times and Siena College released October 3, Paxton is trailing Talarico by six percentage points.

Trump's comments on Paxton's appearance appear to be a recurring pattern.

Speaking to HuffPost, Dan Cassino, a professor of political science at Fairleigh Dickinson University, said Trump has consistently equated outward signs of masculinity with strength in leadership.

"At the end of the day, Trump has a very clear sense of what a good candidate is, what a good candidate looks like," Cassino said. "In his mind, the ideal candidate is male, tall, handsome, dresses the way he thinks they should be dressed. If you don't fit that mold, or if you fall short of that stereotype in any way, then Trump doesn't see you as a viable candidate."

Trump also frequently comments on his own appearance. While speaking in Nebraska on Monday, he claimed supporters had told him he looked to be in tremendous shape and had more of a presidential look than former Presidents George Washington and Abraham Lincoln.

During his first presidential term in 2016, he asked a crowd: "I have a very great presidential look. Do I look like a president? I think I look like a president... Am I good looking?"

"When Trump endorses someone or campaigns with them, and they don't live up to his standards, that's when this mindset becomes an issue," Cassino said. "His comments [about Paxton] reflect that he believes Paxton isn't masculine enough, so he doesn't look like a good candidate or someone who can win."

Is Trump being intentional with his comments about Paxton?

Brandon Rottinghaus, a political science professor at the University of Houston, believes Trump may be laying the groundwork in case Paxton loses.

"At the end of the day, the question is: who takes the blame? The president might be creating a scenario where Paxton is responsible for any potential losses in that state," Rottinghaus said. "Trump doesn't want to be the one blamed for Republican electoral losses."

Rottinghaus stressed that was just his personal speculation though.

"The president's strategy has always been unpredictable because he's loose-lipped on these issues. Paxton needs Trump's endorsement and support, and Trump is happy to make Paxton a laughingstock," he said.

Josh Blank, director of the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas at Austin, offered two other interpretations. The first is that the comments could simply be a reflection of his frustrations with the trouble Paxton has caused for Republicans.

"If the president is hyper-focused on Ken Paxton's negative characteristics, it might just be venting frustrations," Blank told HuffPost.

Alternatively, the comments could give voters a harmless flaw to focus on, "so that voters can absolve themselves while continuing to support him, acknowledging his shortcomings."

Paxton has faced multiple allegations throughout his political career, including securities fraud, corruption, bribery, abuse of office and retaliation against whistleblowers. Blank also noted that Paxton has refused to debate Talarico.

"This is not a normal race," Blank said. "And if Republicans start behaving weirdly in the final months of the race, it's because they're not used to being in this position."

Cal Jillson, a political science professor at Southern Methodist University who specializes in Texas politics, said Paxton's base is very likely to continue to back him.

Speaking about Paxton, Jillson said: "I was talking to an old friend yesterday and he said: 'You know, he's a crook, but he's our crook.' That kind of sums up the feelings of the Republican base perfectly."

Why does this election matter?

Paxton is a household name in Texas. After a decade in the state Legislature, he was elected attorney general in 2014. He has been a steadfast supporter of the "Make America Great Again" (MAGA) movement since 2016, and has received millions of dollars in campaign contributions through a new political action committee based in Texas and tied to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, "MAGA Inc." as well as other Republican organizations.

Jillson noted that a loss would have far deeper implications. "If Paxton loses and the governor's race is incredibly, incredibly tight, the consequences will be catastrophic."

As of publication time, Paxton's team did not respond to HuffPost's request for comment.

Zach Kraft, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee, told HuffPost in a statement: "President Trump has called Ken Paxton the greatest attorney general in history and made it clear he will do everything he can to help him become the next U.S. Senator from Texas. As Texans learn more about James Talarico's radical agenda — eliminating the oil and gas industry, raising taxes and forcing gender transitions on children — they are increasingly clear that they absolutely do not want anything to do with this guy."
